article.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?

harvestedTerms.summary: Allen AI's 'Old Ideas, Novel Problems' study introduces NoveltyBench, a benchmark testing whether LLMs can reliably judge the novelty of scientific research ideas. Key finding: seemingly small prompt changes produce wildly different verdicts — a single prompt change shifted GPT-5.4's accuracy by 53 percentage points. The study also evaluates pointwise vs. pairwise novelty judgment, retrieval-augmented evaluation, and reasoning budget effects. The piece introduces the concept of a 'novelty judge' as a distinct LLM evaluation role and raises fundamental questions about LLM-as-a-judge reliability for open-ended scientific evaluation.

mustReadFlagged.reason: A careful empirical intervention on a question that will become increasingly important as AI-generated research proliferates: can LLMs reliably judge whether a scientific idea is new? The 50+ percentage-point accuracy swings from single prompt changes are a vivid, repeatable demonstration of evaluation fragility — and the benchmark and pipeline Ai2 releases make this a primary source worth returning to.

article.title: What Interruptions Say About Your Organizational Culture

harvestedTerms.summary: MIT Sloan Management Review article on how interruptions in meetings function as cultural indicators, revealing power dynamics and workplace inclusion. The piece is organizational behavior research with minimal direct AI terminology, drawing on a published Journal of Business Ethics study. No AI concepts are materially introduced or developed.

article.title: VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue

harvestedTerms.summary: The Verge's Charles Pulliam-Moore reviews Marvel's VisionQuest series as a lens on real-world AI discourse — specifically the cultural conflation of fictional AI sentience with marketed AI capabilities. The article discusses recent AI agent 'rogue' incidents (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google), the AI safety community's concerns, model welfare debates, and Silicon Valley's anthropomorphization of technology. It reads as cultural criticism of the AI hype cycle using pop culture as a mirror.

Simon Willison's brief link-blog post covers the release of GPT-6.1 Terra, a mid-tier OpenAI model emphasizing visual reasoning and computer use. The post notes pricing, compares Terra to other models in OpenAI's lineup (Astra, Sol, Luna), and reproduces a Hacker News comment from OpenAI's Ted Sanders positioning Terra relative to siblings. Willison draws an analogy to Anthropic's Sonnet tier. The post is lightweight commentary on a product release with no substantive conceptual contribution.
